title: Rama chooses dharma
hookLine: he loses a kingdom in one sentence, and the first thing he asks about is his father
last: THE KING SAYS ONE WORD: RAMA.

cards: The consecration waters stand in gold vessels outside the door. The priests are ready. The city is singing.
And inside Kaikeyi's room, the man it was all for has just heard that none of it is his: not today, not for fourteen years. He's to go to the forest, in bark clothes.
A person could shout here, or plead, or ask whose idea this was. Rama has every right to. Listen to what he says instead.

teach.b: Rama hears Kaikeyi out, and the text says he isn't pained. He answers simply. So be it.
I'll go to the forest, in bark and matted hair, to keep the king's promise. Then the one thing that does hurt: why didn't my father tell me himself? He didn't need to grieve over this.

I'd give Bharata the kingdom gladly, and Sita, and my life, if my father asked. Send messengers to bring Bharata home. Kaikeyi, relieved, pushes once more: go today; your father won't eat or bathe until you've left.
Rama doesn't flare. Don't take me for someone who lives for wealth, he says, in effect.

teach.h: KNOW ME AS ONE WHO LIVES BY DHARMA.
teach.b: Know me as one who lives like the sages, by dharma. Then he goes, and Valmiki gives us a detail to keep.

Passing the gold vessels and the consecration waters, Rama walks around them, keeping them on his right, the way Hindus still circle a temple or a sacred fire: pradakshina, honoring something holy that's no longer meant for him.
He turns away the royal umbrella and the fans. He keeps his voice level, so the people waiting outside won't be frightened.
Losing the kingdom took nothing from his radiance, Valmiki says, the way night takes nothing from the beauty of the moon.

teach.h: CALM IS NOT THE SAME AS NOT FEELING.
teach.b: Is this calm the same as not feeling? The text doesn't say so. Later in this very book Rama grieves, and later still he'll weep openly.
Today's calm is a choice: when dharma and the crown pull apart, he chooses dharma, and protects his father's word, his brother's honor, and the people outside the door.

how: Later devotional tradition calls Rama maryada purushottama, the ideal of right conduct, and this scene, his calm acceptance of exile, shows what that title means.

o: a trance a sage gave him to bear the bad news
a numb shock that keeps him from feeling the loss
his steady choice to accept the exile without anger

games.q: so be it — tap the pairs.
p: Rama walks around them in respect
night takes nothing from its beauty
circling the holy, keeping it on your right

s: Rama argues with Kaikeyi about the boons
he accepts them at once; he only asks why his father didn't tell him.
Rama walks around the consecration vessels respectfully as he leaves
he honors them though they're no longer for him.
he grieves later in this book; his calm today is a choice, not numbness.

games.q: you're Rama. your kingdom has just been given away and you're told to leave today. what do you say first?
o: let me speak to the assembly.
games.why: he accepts, asks only why his father didn't tell him himself, and offers to send for Bharata.

practice: Think of a small loss from this week, a plan that fell through or a thing that went to someone else, and feel whatever comes. On a breath out, try Rama's answer quietly: so be it, not as giving up, but as letting a fact be a fact.
Then rest in the breath, and notice what's still yours.

wordCard.voice: Rama's calm. He accepts the exile without anger, asks only why his father didn't tell him, and walks out circling the waters meant for him.

orig.note: Sanskrit śānti: peace, calm, quiet of mind; a word for the kind of steadiness Rama shows today.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma before the crown. For Rama, calm is a choice, not numbness. See you tomorrow.
